title: Problema III — Was it ethically defensible for Abraham to keep silent about his undertaking to Sarah, to Eliezer and to Isaac?

slots.text: The ethical as such is the universal, and, as the universal, it is in turn what is disclosed. Taken in his immediacy — as a being of senses and soul — the single individual is the concealed one. His ethical task, then, is to work himself free of his concealment — his state of being hidden — and to become disclosed in the universal. So every time he wants to remain in concealment, he sins and is in a spiritual trial, and he can come out of it only by disclosing himself.

Here we stand once again at the same point. If there is no concealment that has its ground in this — that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — then Abraham’s conduct cannot be defended; for he passed over the intermediate ethical authorities. If, on the other hand, there is such a concealment, then we stand before the paradox, which cannot be mediated, since it rests precisely on the single individual’s being, as the single individual, higher than the universal — but the universal is precisely mediation. The Hegelian philosophy assumes no justified concealment, no justified incommensurability. It is therefore consistent with itself when it demands disclosure — that the individual bring what is hidden in him out into the open, and make himself known. But it is confused when it wants to regard Abraham as the father of faith and to talk about faith. For faith is not the first immediacy but a later one. The first immediacy is the aesthetic, and here the Hegelian philosophy may well be right. But faith is not the aesthetic — or else there has never been faith, because there has always been faith.

The best course here will be to consider the whole matter purely aesthetically, and to that end to enter into an aesthetic deliberation. I would ask the reader to give himself over to it completely for the time being, while I, to do my part, will adapt my presentation to its subjects. The category I want to consider a little more closely is the interesting — what stands at a crisis, where things hang in the balance. It is a category that has gained great importance, especially in our time, precisely because the age lives in discrimine rerum — at a turning point in affairs; for it is really the category of the turning point. So one should not, as sometimes happens, first love it oneself pro virili — to the best of one’s powers — and then scorn it because it has grown beyond one. But neither should one be all too greedy for it. For this much is certain: to become interesting, or to have an interesting life, is not a task for artful industry but a fateful privilege, which can be bought only at the price of deep pain, as can every privilege in the world of spirit. Thus Socrates was the most interesting human being who has ever lived, and his life the most interesting ever led; but this existence was assigned to him by the god, and insofar as he had to acquire it himself, he was no stranger to toil and pain either. To want to take such an existence in vain is unbecoming for anyone who thinks at all seriously about life; and yet in our time one not infrequently sees examples of such striving. The interesting, moreover, is a border category, a confinium — a borderland — between aesthetics and ethics. To that extent the deliberation must constantly stray over into the territory of ethics, while, if it is to have any significance, it must seize the problem with aesthetic inwardness and concupiscence. In our time ethics seldom engages in such things. The reason is said to be that there can be no room for them in the System. Well then, one could do it in monographs. And besides, if one does not want to be long-winded about it, one can do it briefly and still achieve the same thing — provided, that is, that one has the predicate in one’s power; for one or two predicates can betray a whole world. Is there to be no room in the System for such little words either?

Aristotle says in his immortal Poetics: δύο μὲν οὖν τοῦ μύθου μέρη, περὶ ταῦτ’ ἐστί, περιπέτεια καὶ ἀναγνώρισις — two parts of the plot, then, turn on these things: peripeteia, the reversal, and anagnorisis, the recognition (cf. chapter 11). Naturally it is only the second element that concerns me here: ἀναγνώρισις, recognition. Wherever there can be talk of a recognition, there is eo ipso — by that very fact — talk of a preceding concealment. Just as the recognition is what resolves, what releases the tension, so the concealment is what builds the suspense, the tension, in dramatic life. Earlier in the same chapter Aristotle develops the differing worth of tragedies according to how περιπέτεια and ἀναγνώρισις carom off each other, and discusses single and double recognition. I cannot take account of that here, however much it tempts by its inwardness and its quiet absorption — especially someone who has long enough been wearied by the superficial omniscience of the survey-writers. A more general remark must find its place here. In Greek tragedy, concealment (and, as a consequence, recognition) is an epic remnant. It has its ground in a fate in which the dramatic action vanishes, and from which that action has its dark, enigmatic origin. That is why the effect a Greek tragedy produces resembles the impression a marble statue makes, lacking as it does the power of the eye. Greek tragedy is blind. That is why a certain abstraction is required in order to be properly affected by it. A son murders his father, but only afterward does he learn that it was his father. A sister is about to sacrifice her brother, but at the decisive moment she finds out. This kind of tragedy can have less hold on our reflective age. Modern drama has given up fate; it has emancipated itself dramatically; it is sighted; it gazes into itself and takes fate up into its dramatic consciousness. Concealment and disclosure are then the hero’s free act, for which he is responsible.

In modern drama, too, recognition and concealment belong as an essential element. To cite examples of this would be too long-winded. I am polite enough to assume that anyone in our time who is so aesthetically voluptuous, so potent and so inflamed that he conceives as easily as the partridge, which, according to Aristotle, needs only to hear the cock’s voice or his flight over her head — I assume that anyone, merely on hearing the word “concealment,” will easily be able to shake ten or so novels and comedies out of his sleeve. I can therefore be brief and so straight away merely indicate a more general remark. If the one who plays hide-and-seek, and thereby brings dramatic ferment into the play, is hiding some nonsense, we get a comedy; if, however, he stands in relation to the idea, he can come close to being a tragic hero. Here is just one example of the comic. A man wears makeup and a wig. This same man would dearly like to make a conquest of the fair sex, and he is quite sure of victory with the help of the makeup and the wig, which render him unconditionally irresistible. He catches a girl and stands on the summit of happiness. Now comes the catch. Can he confess it? Will he not lose all his bewitching power when he shows himself as a plain, ordinary — indeed, even a bald — male person? Will he not thereby lose his beloved again? — His concealment is his free act, for which aesthetics, too, holds him responsible. This science is no friend of bald hypocrites; it hands him over to laughter. This must be enough merely to indicate what I mean; the comic cannot be the object of this investigation’s interest.

The path I have to take is to carry concealment dialectically through aesthetics and ethics; for the point is that aesthetic concealment and the paradox should show themselves in their absolute difference.

A couple of examples. A girl is secretly in love with someone, though the two of them have not definitively confessed their love to each other. Her parents compel her to marry another man (there may, besides, be a consideration of filial piety that decides her); she obeys her parents; she hides her love “so as not to make the other unhappy, and no one shall ever know what she suffers.” — A young man could, by a single word, come into possession of the object of his longings and his restless dreams. This little word, however, would compromise — indeed perhaps (who knows?) ruin — an entire family. He magnanimously resolves to remain in hiding: “The girl shall never know it, so that she may perhaps become happy at another man’s hand.” A pity that these two people, each of whom is hidden from his or her respective beloved, are also hidden from each other; otherwise a remarkable higher unity could have been brought about here. — Their concealment is a free act, for which they are responsible to aesthetics as well. Aesthetics, however, is a polite and sentimental science, which knows more ways out than any manager of the public pawnshop. So what does it do? It does everything possible for the lovers. By means of a coincidence, the respective partners in the projected marriage get a hint of the other party’s magnanimous resolution; an explanation follows; they get each other, and along with that the rank of real heroes. For although they have not even had time to sleep on their heroic resolution, aesthetics nevertheless regards it as if they had bravely fought their purpose through for many years. Aesthetics, you see, does not care much about time; whether in jest or in earnest, time goes equally fast for it.

But ethics knows nothing of that coincidence or of that sentimentality, nor does it have so quick a notion of time. This gives the matter a different look. Ethics is not good to argue with, since its categories are pure. It does not invoke experience — of all ridiculous things just about the most ridiculous — which, far from making a man wise, is more likely to make him mad if he knows nothing higher. Ethics has no coincidence, and so no explanation follows. It does not trifle with dignities. It lays an enormous responsibility on the slender heroes’ shoulders. It condemns as presumptuous the wish to play Providence by one’s deed — but it also condemns the wish to do so by one’s suffering. It bids one believe in actuality and have the courage to fight with all the tribulations of actuality, rather than with these bloodless sufferings one has taken upon oneself on one’s own responsibility. It warns against believing the clever calculations of the understanding, which are more faithless than the oracles of antiquity. It warns against every untimely magnanimity. Leave it to actuality: then it is time to show courage — but then ethics itself offers every possible assistance. If, however, it was something deeper that stirred in these two, if there was earnestness to see the task, earnestness to take it up, then something will no doubt come of them; but ethics cannot help them. It has taken offense; for they have a secret from it, a secret they have taken on at their own risk and on their own answer.
Aesthetics, then, demanded concealment and rewarded it; ethics demanded disclosure and punished concealment.

Sometimes, however, aesthetics itself demands disclosure. When the hero, caught in the aesthetic illusion, thinks that by his silence he is saving another human being, aesthetics demands silence and rewards it. When, on the other hand, the hero by his deed intervenes disruptively in another human being’s life, it demands disclosure. Here I have arrived at the tragic hero. I want to consider Euripides’ Iphigenia in Aulis for a moment. Agamemnon is to sacrifice Iphigenia. Now, aesthetics demands silence of Agamemnon insofar as it would be unworthy of the hero to look for comfort from anyone else — just as he ought, out of consideration for the women, to hide it from them for as long as possible. On the other hand, precisely in order to be a hero, the hero must also be put to the proof in the terrible spiritual trial that the tears of Clytemnestra and Iphigenia will prepare for him. What does aesthetics do? It has a way out: it has an old servant ready, who discloses everything to Clytemnestra. Now everything is in order.

Ethics, however, has no coincidence and no old servant at hand. The aesthetic idea contradicts itself as soon as it has to be carried out in actuality. Ethics therefore demands disclosure. The tragic hero shows his ethical courage precisely in this: that he, caught in no aesthetic illusion, is himself the one who announces her fate to Iphigenia. If he does this, then the tragic hero is the beloved son of ethics, in whom it is well pleased. Should he keep silent, that may be because he believes he makes it easier for others by doing so; but it may also be because he makes it easier for himself by doing so. Of this, however, he knows himself to be free. If he keeps silent, he takes on a responsibility as the single individual, insofar as he disregards an argument that may come from outside. This, as a tragic hero, he cannot do; for the very reason ethics loves him is that he always expresses the universal. His heroic deed demands courage, but it also belongs to this courage that he shirks no argument. Now it is certain that tears are a terrible argumentum ad hominem — an argument aimed at the man himself — and there has surely been someone whom nothing touched, yet whom tears moved. In the play Iphigenia is allowed to weep. In actuality she ought to be granted, like Jephthah’s daughter, two months to weep — not in solitude but at her father’s feet — and to use all the art she has, “which is only tears,” and to twine herself, instead of an olive branch, around his knees (cf. line 1224).
Aesthetics demanded disclosure but made do with a coincidence; ethics demanded disclosure and found its satisfaction in the tragic hero.

In spite of the strictness with which ethics demands disclosure, it cannot be denied that secrecy and silence are what really make a human being great, precisely because they are determinations of inwardness. When Amor leaves Psyche, he says to her: “You shall give birth to a child who will be divine if you keep silent, but a human being if you betray the secret.” The tragic hero, who is the favorite of ethics, is purely a human being; him I can indeed understand, and everything he undertakes also lies in what is disclosed, out in the open. If I go further, I keep coming up against the paradox — the divine and the demonic; for silence is both. Silence is the snare of the demon, and the more silence is kept, the more terrible the demon grows; but silence is also the deity’s co-witnessing with the single individual.

Before I go on to the story of Abraham, however, I will call forth a couple of poetic individualities. By the power of dialectic I keep them on the point, and as I swing the scourge of despair over them, I will surely keep them from standing still, so that, if possible, in their anxiety they may discover one thing or another.

notes.text: These movements and positions might well still become the object of aesthetic treatment; but whether faith’s movements and positions, and the whole life of faith, can become so, I leave undecided here. Only, since it always gives me joy to thank whomever I owe something, I want to thank Lessing for the scattered hints about a Christian drama that are found in his Hamburgische Dramaturgie (Hamburg Dramaturgy). He, however, fixed his gaze on the purely divine side of this life (the completed victory), and therefore he despaired; perhaps he would have judged otherwise had he paid more attention to the purely human side (theologia viatorum — the theology of those still on the way). What he says is admittedly very brief, and partly evasive; but since I am always exceedingly glad when I can get an occasion to bring Lessing in, I take it at once. Lessing was not only one of the most comprehensive minds Germany has possessed; he not only had a quite rare readiness in his knowledge, which means that one can safely rely on him and on his autopsy — his own firsthand inspection — without fear of being fooled by loose quotations that belong nowhere, by half-understood phrases fetched from unreliable compendia, or of being led astray by a stupid trumpeting of novelties that older writers set out far better — but he also had a most uncommon gift for explaining what he himself had understood. There he stopped; in our time people go further, and explain more than they themselves have understood.

slots.text: Aristotle, in his Politics, relates a story of political unrest in Delphi that arose from a question of marriage. The bridegroom, to whom the augurs foretell a misfortune that will spring from his marriage, abruptly alters his plan at the decisive moment, when he arrives to fetch the bride — he will not have the wedding. I need no more. In Delphi this event hardly passed off without tears; if a poet wanted to take it up, he could surely count on sympathy. Is it not terrible that love, which often enough has been an exile in life, is now robbed of heaven’s help as well? Is the old saying that marriages are made in heaven not put to shame here? At other times it is all the tribulations and difficulties of finitude that, like evil spirits, would separate the lovers; but love has heaven on its side, and that is why this holy alliance conquers all its enemies. Here it is heaven itself that separates what heaven itself, after all, has joined. And who would have suspected this? Least of all, surely, the young bride. Only a moment ago she was sitting in her room in all her beauty. The lovely girls had adorned her so conscientiously that they could answer for it before all the world, so that it gave them not only joy but envy — indeed, joy that they could not possibly grow more envious, because she could not possibly be more beautiful. Alone in her room she sat, transformed from beauty to beauty; for everything feminine art could do had been used to adorn worthily the one who was worthy. Yet something was still missing, something the young girls had not dreamed of: a veil finer, lighter and yet more concealing than the one in which the young girls had wrapped her; a bridal garment that no young girl knew about or could help her with — indeed, the bride herself did not have the understanding to help herself. It was an invisible power, a kindly power that takes its delight in adorning a bride, that wrapped her in it without her knowing anything about it; for she saw only how the bridegroom went past and went up to the temple. She saw the door close behind him, and she grew even calmer and more blessed, for she knew he was now hers more than ever. The temple door opened, he stepped out; but she lowered her eyes, as a maiden does, and so she did not see that his face was distraught. But he saw that heaven was surely envious of the bride’s loveliness and of his happiness. The temple door opened, and the young girls saw the bridegroom step out; but they did not see that his face was distraught, for they were busy fetching the bride. Then she came forth in all her maidenly humility, and yet like a sovereign lady, surrounded by her retinue of young girls, who curtsied to her as a young girl always curtsies to a bride. So she stood at the head of the lovely band and waited — it was only a moment, for the temple was right nearby — and the bridegroom came — but he went past her door.

notes.anchorAfterEn: he will not have the wedding. I need no more.
notes.text: According to Aristotle, the historical catastrophe was as follows: to take revenge, the family gets a temple vessel in among his household goods, and he is condemned as a temple robber. This, however, is of no importance; for the question is not whether the family is clever or stupid in taking its revenge. The family has ideal significance only insofar as it is drawn into the hero’s dialectic. Besides, it is fateful enough that, in trying to escape the danger by not marrying, he plunges into it, and that his life touches the divine in two ways: first through the augur’s pronouncement, then by being condemned as a temple robber.
